question.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

Consider the vector space $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ of all $2 \times 2$ matrices over $\mathbb{R}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235559/assets/69a6afc9d6a71cbdaf0bc828532b6ba09c8cd71759f3980711dd05a7064eb263.svg) is a linearly independent set in $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$

II. $[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235559/assets/221ac2c0a61b8b89b144b919554779217ce4f61ecb02aa17c89bd4a5f9780997.svg)

III. ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235559/assets/05ed6d1fba6ff07b880d80d10e12927abbc08f1ef12b7b015d41e830ade26d97.svg) is a basis of $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$
current_example.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235559/assets/f60ce409421657f351da8646559a9ef0783071367721ac874738eff0e10c4631.svg)
is true if and only if $x_1=x_2=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235559/assets/d1fe442d52dd2a91b30c01ab68f35f919c981f7746cc73590b951878e7bf821b.svg)

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235559/assets/1c8961a64ee9df3f2e8ac97d77a2052ffe81f0604eb8bc118a5808e1dc9c12b9.svg)
since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry $a_{11} = 0\mathbin{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235559/assets/30504faf7aae5213793f3741199242f80986c730358dbaab084648529bdfa5ec.svg)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."
